articles.title: ‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new film
articles.summary: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV. A man from Long Beach, California, is here to have sex with someone he believes is a 13-year-old girl. When the journalist Chris Hansen walks in, the man’s stomach drops.
body: This is the opening scene of Primetime, a film directed by Lance Oppenheim, released in the US this week (a UK release follows on 30 October). It explores how a network news show turned sting operations into must-see television, raising a host of ethical questions about justice, voyeurism and society’s willingness to dehumanise certain offenders for profit and entertainment.

The swaggering Hansen is played by Robert Pattinson, whose recent movies include The Batman, The Drama and The Odyssey. He delivers a line that captures the film’s argument about a societal turning point: “There used to be a pillory in every village. Now, there’s a television in every living room.” But the real Hansen, 67, has branded the movie an “insult” and “identity theft” without having seen it.

articles.title: Meryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues?
articles.summary: The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators. It is a confusing time to be alive, given how often these days Hollywood indulges in revisionism.
body: News that the Oscar-winner might be portraying Narnia’s Christ-like big cat first surfaced in April last year, prompting a flurry of complaints from conservative Christians. This week, the naysayers were back after Empire published a first look at the film, along with an interview with Gerwig in which the director confirmed the casting and explained her choice of actor. Streep, it turns out, was hired not because the Barbie director desperately fancied stoking the flames of controversy, but because she needed someone over 70 who could convey both wisdom and childlike wonder.

“I wanted someone who was profound but not pretentious, who had gravitas but not morose self-seriousness,” Gerwig said. She also explained she wanted one of the finest actors working today, adding: “That list is not a long one.”

articles.title: RioFilme to Announce $20 Million Film and TV Incentives at Rio Film Fest’s RioMarket
articles.summary: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — RioFilme, the film and TV company of Rio de Janeiro City, will launch a call for proposals amounting to R$100 million ($20 million) for film and TV show production, development, distribution and international co-productions, Leonardo Edde, president of RioFilme, told…
body: A minimum of 12 documentary productions, including theatrical, TV or streaming works, will receive a total of $2.4 million. A further $1 million in development funding will be available to 20 projects for cinema, TV and streaming, while a total of $1.2 million is destined to fund the distribution of a minimum of 12 feature films.
The novelty of this year’s incentive package, said Edde, is a $3 million line for at least four international co-production projects of fiction and animated feature films.

The first five lines are for productions in which a Rio-based company is the leading producer, he added. For the co-production line, however, projects in which local companies have a minority stake are also eligible, Edde stressed.

The co-production funding is part of a plan to consolidate Rio as a major world film and TV production hub. Rio has streamlined its film commission and created incentives that has made it one of the most filmed cities in the world, surpassing Paris and Mexico City in terms of days shot in the city. In the first half of 2026, Rio hosted 40 international productions, up from 28 in the same period last year, Edde added.

articles.title: ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film
articles.summary: Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen. Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.
body: It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign by Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.

“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”

It prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.

The result, nine years later, is The Lost Children of Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.

articles.title: ‘Charlie Harper’ Review: Emilia Jones and Nick Robinson Come Apart, in Fits and Starts, in a Fuzzy, Non-Linear Breakup Drama
articles.summary: The first thing to know about “Charlie Harper” is that it’s not, in fact, about someone called Charlie Harper. Charlie (Nick Robinson) and Harper (Emilia Jones) are a couple, meeting and parting at various stages across a five-year timeline; the title of this earnestly melancholy first feature by…
body: The stars are appealing enough in Mac Eldridge and Tom Dean's directorial debut, but can't quite make us care about the ill-starred couple they play.

We begin, naturally, somewhere in the middle: Our introduction to the principals is not theirs to each other. When Charlie approaches Harper in a low-lit bar to introduce himself, she says they’ve met before, jogging his memory about their first encounter way back in high school. But this is just another round of a game they’ve played before, with the shoe on the other foot, and when we circle back to that same scene toward the close, we’re more conscious of the weight of what has transpired between them. Starting over as strangers would be sweeter and easier.

articles.title: Patti LaBelle, Common, Public Enemy Honored at Black Music Action Coalition Gala 2026
articles.summary: Patti LaBelle, Common and Public Enemy were among the artists and executives who were celebrated on Thursday night at the sixth annual Black Music Action Coalition Gala, held at the Beverly Hilton Hotel in Los Angeles.
body: Director Lee Daniels took the podium to dedicate the Icon Award to LaBelle, sharing how her presence in his life helped him overcome his battle with addiction. “Your voice is healing. Your voice is power, your voice is soul,” he said. “When I first heard your music, I was 22 years old. It changed my life, and I knew I wanted to be an artist.”

LaBelle then thanked BMAC and shared how grateful she was to be honored at the age of 82. “I want you to know that music is medicine,” she said. “We all need that medicine, especially now that we’re going through all these trying times. Music is my life, and music will heal us all. And thank God we’re all here and that we all woke up this morning.”

One of the more emotional moments of the evening came when Dr. Mahalia Hines introduced her son, rapper Common, who received the Harry Belafonte Change Agent Award. She commended him for his activism and willingness to perform concerts and hold conversations with incarcerated individuals across the United States.

articles.title: My dad was a monster! Sara Karloff on reviving Frankenstein, 95 years on
articles.summary: Boris Karloff’s daughter and composer Michael Shapiro, whose musical score for the 1931 film is finally coming to London, talk about how it became a much-loved classic.
body: Once seen, never forgotten – the 1931 Frankenstein is 95 years old, but still one of the most instantly recognisable of classic horrors. Whether it’s the sight of lanky Boris Karloff lumbering into the frame with his squared-off head, neck bolts and oversized leaden shoes, or the sound of a thunderclap and Colin Clive exclaiming “It’s alive!” as the monster comes to life one stormy night in the laboratory – the film still raises hairs on the back of the neck.

However, this classic has arguably long been missing one element: a continuous musical soundtrack – the original movie had dialogue but no music. In 2001, the American composer Michael Shapiro wrote a full-length score, which he will be conducting alongside the film for the first time in London next month, at Cadogan Hall with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. “It becomes one artistic expression, one artistic experience,” he says. “The film and the music, together, and the audience forgets that I am there.” Shapiro says his music emphasises what is already up on the screen. “Suddenly the film jumps out in a way it never did before.”

articles.title: Ed Sheeran's next US concerts cancelled due to storm warning
articles.summary: The star's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday are cancelled after severe weather warnings.
body: Ed Sheeran's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday have been cancelled because of severe weather warnings in the area.
The singer had been scheduled to perform two shows at the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, near Boston, as part of his current US tour.

The tour has been in the headlines because of a row over a decision to drop Sheeran's support act Macklemore for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Stadium owners including the Gillette Stadium's Robert Kraft lobbied for his removal.

A statement from the venue, external said: "Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, the promoter and tour have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium."

articles.title: Some BBC channels and radio stations may well have to close, director general says
articles.summary: The BBC's financial situation "may well mean" some channels and stations close, Matt Brittin says.
body: The BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services, its director general has said.
As the BBC seeks £500m savings, Matt Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".
He said: "The tight financial situation means that we're having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like."
Audience behaviour is also rapidly changing, he said. "If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look at the value and the cost of all of those different services."
points: The BBC's financial situation "may well mean" some channels and stations close, Matt Brittin says.

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s ‘9 to 5’ Comedy Returning to Theaters to Support Late Icon’s Foundation
articles.summary: The weeklong theatrical run from Oct. 9 will see net proceeds from ticket sales supporting the flagship Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library launched by the late Queen of Country Music.
body: Walt Disney is sending the classic 1980 workplace comedy 9 to 5 back to theaters next month for a weeklong run, with net proceeds from ticket sales supporting the Dollywood Foundation after Dolly Parton died last month at age 80.

Inspired by her father’s inability to read and write, Parton created the book-gifting charity to promote literacy among young people in their earliest years. Since its founding in 1995, the program has given over 300 million free books to children across North American, the UK, Australia and the Republic of Ireland.

Parton, known as the Queen of Country music, died after a brief battle with cancer. The 9 to 5 theatrical re-release was announced on the inaugural Give Like Dolly Day, a new annual celebration set for Sept. 25, or 9/25, a date chosen as an homage to the comedy film.

9 to 5, directed by Colin Higgins and about women office workers seeking revenge against the man making their lives miserable, included the “9 to 5” protest song penned and sung by Parton, and for which she received an Academy Award nomination.
